findings.question: STUN/TURN server options: Self-hosted Coturn (server specs for 1000 clients, bandwidth GB/month, deployment complexity), Cloudflare Calls (pricing, limits, latency, SLA), Twilio TURN (pricing, reliability), Public STUN (reliability, limits, privacy), verdict for MONOTERMINAL
findings.answer: SELF-HOSTED COTURN: 1000 concurrent clients requires 2-4 vCPU + 2-4 GB RAM (relay traffic CPU-light, mostly forwarding), bandwidth 50-200 GB/month (calculation: 1000 * 10% TURN * 100 KB/s * 30 days * 86400s ≈ 260 GB), deployment MEDIUM complexity (Docker coturn/coturn, turnserver.conf realm+ports+credentials, firewall UDP 3478 + TCP 3478 + UDP 49152-65535), cost $10-30/month VPS (DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Vultr). CLOUDFLARE CALLS: Pricing $0.05/GB relayed (2024, verify 2026), 1000 concurrent limit (Standard plan), latency 5-50ms to regional edge POPs, SLA 99.9% uptime, global anycast + auto-scaling + dashboard, cost estimate 100 GB/month = $5 / 1 TB/month = $50. TWILIO TURN: Pricing $0.0004/min active connection (~$0.024/hour), 1000 concurrent * 10% TURN * 24h * 30d * $0.024 = $1728/month (expensive!), reliability 99.95% SLA, API complexity REST for time-limited tokens, NOT cost-effective for persistent terminal sessions. PUBLIC STUN (Google): Free stun.l.google.com:19302 + stun1-4.l.google.com:19302, reliability 95-99% uptime (no SLA, best-effort), usage limits undocumented rate-limited per IP (safe <1000 clients/IP), privacy Google sees client IPs (STUN reveals public IP), suitable STUN-only NOT TURN relay. VERDICT MONOTERMINAL: MVP self-hosted Coturn on $15/month VPS (full control, predictable cost), backup Google public STUN (free fallback), scale Cloudflare Calls if relay traffic >500 GB/month ($25+ cheaper than VPS bandwidth), avoid Twilio TURN (70x more expensive).

findings.question: Hole punching techniques: UDP hole punching success rate % by router type (cone NAT, symmetric NAT, CGNAT), timing requirements, TCP hole punching feasibility, STUN binding mechanism, TURN relay fallback (latency overhead ms, bandwidth cost, trigger after Y attempts), mobile cellular considerations (CGNAT %, IPv6 %, dynamic IP)
findings.answer: UDP HOLE PUNCHING SUCCESS: Full Cone NAT 95-99% (accepts any external packet after outbound), Restricted Cone NAT 90-95% (requires source IP match), Port-Restricted Cone 85-90% (requires source IP+port match), Symmetric NAT 30-50% (randomizes ports, race condition needed), Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) 20-40% (double NAT, rare alignment). Timing requirement <2s race condition for symmetric NAT (both peers send packets simultaneously, ICE coordination ensures this via STUN Binding). Algorithm: (1) STUN Binding reveals external IP:port, (2) exchange via signaling, (3) both peers send to each other's external address, (4) NAT creates mappings, packets traverse. TCP HOLE PUNCHING: Feasibility LOWER 30-50% symmetric NAT (TCP requires SYN-ACK handshake, timing harder, some NAT/firewalls drop simultaneous TCP SYN), implementation complexity HIGH (requires simultaneous SYN with matching sequence numbers, Linux SO_REUSEADDR + connect() tricks), not widely used due to reliability issues. Recommendation: Use UDP hole punching, fallback to TURN for TCP-like reliability. STUN BINDING: (1) Client sends STUN Binding Request to server, (2) server responds with client's reflexive (external) IP:port, (3) client learns NAT mapping, shares with peer via signaling. Success detection: Binding response <500ms = success, >500ms suggests packet loss/restrictive NAT, no response after 3 retries (1s, 2s, 4s) = STUN failure. Failure scenarios: Symmetric NAT changes ports per destination (need TURN), firewall blocks UDP 3478 (need TCP TURN), no internet. TURN RELAY FALLBACK: Latency overhead +50-150ms (Client → TURN → peer = 2 hops vs 1 direct), bandwidth cost 2x relay vs direct (TURN forwards traffic, counted twice ingress+egress), trigger after Y=3 failed hole punch attempts (1s, 2s, 4s backoff), Y=5 more aggressive. Recommended Y=3 (balance latency vs TURN cost). MOBILE CELLULAR: Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) 60-80% of carriers (shared public IP across thousands, hole punching drops to 20-40%, TURN required for majority), IPv6 support 40-60% of carriers 2026 (improves hole punching to 80-85%, no NAT with IPv6, prefer IPv6 when available), dynamic IP changes WiFi ↔ cellular handoff 10-30s interruption (requires ICE restart re-gather candidates + re-punch).

findings.question: Fallback strategies: TURN relay (cost implications $/GB, user notification UX, quality degradation +X ms), Direct IP manual connection (when discovery fails, port forwarding instructions), Hybrid relay (partial P2P cost/benefit), Offline mode (local sessions, sync), Connection quality indicator (states, RTT display thresholds ms)
findings.answer: TURN RELAY: Cost implications $0.05/GB (Cloudflare) or VPS bandwidth, calculation 10 KB/s avg * 3600s * 100 concurrent TURN users = 3.6 GB/hour → $0.05/GB * 3.6 * 720 hours/month = $130/month for 100 TURN users, self-hosted $15/month VPS handles 50-100 concurrent TURN (bandwidth-limited). User notification: 'Connection via relay (slower)' banner, show latency 'Latency: 150ms (via relay)' vs 'Latency: 30ms (direct)'. Quality degradation +50-150ms latency, acceptable for terminal (human perception >100ms), NOT acceptable for gaming/video (needs <50ms). DIRECT IP MANUAL: When discovery fails (corporate firewall blocks STUN/TURN, isolated network no internet), UX flow: (1) Auto-discovery times out 10s, (2) 'Cannot discover master. Enter IP manually?', (3) Form: IP [___] Port [___] [Connect]. Port forwarding instructions: 'Forward TCP port 8022 on your router to 192.168.1.100:8022', include router-specific guides (common brands). HYBRID RELAY (Partial P2P): Master ↔ Client direct, Client ↔ Client via relay, benefit reduces TURN bandwidth (only peer-to-peer traffic relayed), saves 30-50% TURN bandwidth if multi-client sessions common, cost adds 20-30% code complexity (connection type routing). Verdict: DEFER for MVP (complexity not justified initially). OFFLINE MODE: Local sessions only, no remote connections attempted, master daemon runs locally (Unix socket, no P2P listen), client connects localhost only. Sync when connectivity restored: buffer scrollback changes in SQLite, on reconnect push differential updates. UX: 'Offline Mode' indicator (grayed network icon). CONNECTION QUALITY INDICATOR: States - Direct P2P (Green dot, 'Direct (20ms)'), Relay (Yellow dot, 'Relay (120ms)'), Offline (Red dot, 'Offline'), Reconnecting (Spinner, 'Reconnecting... attempt 2/∞'). RTT display: Updated every 5s (PING/PONG), <50ms Excellent (green), 50-100ms Good (green), 100-200ms Fair (yellow), >200ms Poor (orange/red).

findings.question: Connection reliability: Mobile network switches WiFi ↔ cellular (interruption duration sec, reconnection strategy, ICE restart), Laptop sleep/wake (session persistence, peer IP changes, battery optimization), IP address changes (IPv4 DHCP renewal frequency, IPv6 rotation, NAT rebinding, detect+reconnect speed <X sec), Keepalive (ping interval sec, timeout threshold, battery impact mAh/hour), Reconnection UX (seamless background, persistent indicator, explicit retry button)
findings.answer: MOBILE NETWORK SWITCHES: Interruption duration 10-30s typical (iOS 10-20s Network.framework handles gracefully, Android 15-30s less optimized). Reconnection strategy: Immediate retry (attempt reconnect as soon as network changes), backoff (if fails exponential backoff 1s, 2s, 4s, ...), ICE restart (re-gather candidates on new network interface). UX: 'Network changed, reconnecting...' notification. LAPTOP SLEEP/WAKE: Session persistence save connection state to disk ({peer_id, session_id, last_sequence_number, crypto_keys}), on wake re-establish within X=5s target. Challenge: Peer may have changed IP during sleep, solution re-run ICE (STUN binding) to discover new IP. Battery optimization: Don't reconnect if offline >10 minutes (assume user done). IP ADDRESS CHANGES: IPv4 DHCP renewal every 24-72 hours typical, detection socket error (ECONNRESET, ENETUNREACH), response immediate ICE restart. IPv6 address rotation: Privacy extensions rotate every 1-7 days, detection same as IPv4, response ICE restart. NAT rebinding: Router public IP changes (rare <1/month), detection STUN binding returns different reflexive IP, response re-signal to peers. Speed to detect+reconnect: <5s target (detect immediate socket error or failed ping, reconnect 2-5s ICE re-gathering + hole punch). KEEPALIVE: Ping interval every 30s (balance battery vs responsiveness), WebRTC ICE keepalives automatic (every 15-30s), application-level PING message every 30s. Timeout threshold: Disconnect after 3 missed pings (90s total), 2 missed 'Connection unstable' warning, 3 missed 'Disconnected' + auto-reconnect. Battery impact: 30s ping adds ~5-10 mAh/hour overhead. RECONNECTION UX: Seamless background reconnect PREFERRED (best UX), no user action required, small indicator 'Reconnecting...' toast (3s), auto-dismiss on success. Persistent indicator when >3 failures: 'Reconnecting... attempt 4/∞', 'Cancel' button to abort auto-reconnect. Explicit user retry button when auto-reconnect exhausted (10+ attempts): 'Connection failed. [Retry] [Cancel]', user must choose retry or disconnect.

findings.question: Local network discovery: mDNS/Bonjour implementation - protocol details, performance metrics, platform APIs, limitations, mobile battery impact
findings.answer: PROTOCOL (DNS-SD RFC 6763): Service type _monoterminal._tcp.local, multicast to 224.0.0.251:5353 (mDNS). TXT records for metadata (version=1.0.0, sessions=5, capabilities=p2p+clipboard). Query-response pattern: client sends PTR query, master responds with SRV+A/AAAA+TXT records. IMPLEMENTATION: Avahi (Linux) - libavahi-client API (avahi_client_new, avahi_entry_group_new, avahi_entry_group_add_service), Bonjour (macOS/iOS) - dns_sd.h API (DNSServiceRegister, DNSServiceBrowse), DNS-SD (Windows) - dnsapi.dll (DnsServiceRegister), Rust crates: mdns 3.0+ (cross-platform), zeroconf 0.12+ (libavahi/Bonjour bindings). PERFORMANCE: Discovery time 1-5 seconds typical (multicast + response processing), network traffic ~200-500 bytes per announcement (periodic every 30-60s), CPU overhead <1% (passive multicast listening). LIMITATIONS: (1) Same subnet only - routers block multicast 224.0.0.0/24 by default, NO inter-VLAN discovery. (2) Mobile hotspot isolation - iOS/Android hotspot blocks multicast between clients (AP isolation mode), each client sees master but NOT other clients. (3) Corporate networks - many enterprise WiFi block multicast (security policy), requires unicast DNS-SD fallback (DNS Long-Lived Queries RFC 8764). (4) IPv6 multicast - ff02::fb for link-local, may require separate listener. MOBILE: iOS NSNetServiceBrowser (automatic on WiFi, blocks on cellular), Android NsdManager (API 16+, requires android.permission.CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE for receiving), battery impact <5 mAh/hour passive listening (negligible), active browse ~10-20 mAh/hour. MONOTERMINAL RECOMMENDATION: mDNS for LAN-only discovery (home/office), disable on cellular, fallback to directory for internet/corporate.

limitations: Same subnet only (multicast 224.0.0.0/24 blocked by routers)

findings.question: Internet discovery: DHT (libp2p Kademlia) vs centralized directory - architecture, performance, privacy, scalability, hybrid approach
findings.answer: DHT (DISTRIBUTED HASH TABLE - libp2p Kademlia): Each master advertises peer_id to multiaddrs mapping to DHT. Discovery: client queries DHT for master peer_id, receives multiaddrs (IP:port list), attempts direct connection. libp2p Kademlia: XOR distance metric, k=20 buckets, alpha=3 parallel queries. Discovery time 2-10 seconds (depends on hop count, bootstrap node availability). Node count for reliability: 100+ bootstrap nodes for 99% reachability (IPFS uses ~150 bootstrap nodes). NAT complications: DHT nodes need public IP or relay (STUN/TURN), masters behind NAT cannot be DHT bootstrap nodes but can advertise via relay. Advantages: decentralized (no single point of failure), censorship-resistant. Disadvantages: slow (multi-hop lookups), complex NAT traversal, privacy exposure (all masters publicly discoverable). CENTRALIZED DIRECTORY: REST/gRPC API (monoterminal.io/api/masters). Database schema: CREATE TABLE masters (peer_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, multiaddrs TEXT[] NOT NULL, last_seen TIMESTAMP, session_count INTEGER, metadata JSONB); Heartbeat: masters POST /heartbeat every 30s with multiaddrs+metadata, marked offline if last_seen > 2min. API design: GET /api/masters?filters (public/private/unlisted visibility), POST /api/masters (register), DELETE /api/masters (unregister). Authentication: bearer tokens for write operations (register/unregister), public reads. Discovery time <100ms (single HTTPS request + database query). Advantages: fast, simple, visibility control (public/private/unlisted masters). Disadvantages: centralized (single point of failure, requires hosted service), less privacy (service sees all connections). Scalability: PostgreSQL/MySQL handles 10k+ masters easily (<5ms query time with peer_id index). HYBRID APPROACH: (1) Local mDNS first (1-5s, LAN only), (2) Centralized directory fallback (<100ms, internet), (3) DHT optional (2-10s, decentralization purists). Privacy: directory allows visibility flags (public discoverable, private require auth token, unlisted require exact peer_id). MONOTERMINAL VERDICT: Centralized directory for speed+UX (90% use case), optional DHT for decentralization ideology (<10% users), mDNS for LAN. Directory hosted on monoterminal.io, open-source server for self-hosting.

findings.question: Signaling mechanism: WebRTC SDP exchange architecture - signaling server design, message format, security, scalability, fallback strategies
findings.answer: SIGNALING SERVER: WebSocket relay (Node.js/Go/Rust), clients connect via wss://signal.monoterminal.io. Message format: JSON with type (offer/answer/ice), from peer_id, to peer_id, sdp string, candidate RTCIceCandidate. Server is stateless relay (no SDP parsing), just forwards messages peer_id to peer_id. SDP EXCHANGE FLOW: (1) Client A (initiator) creates RTCPeerConnection, generates offer (await pc.createOffer()), sends offer message to signaling server. (2) Server forwards to Client B (responder). (3) Client B creates RTCPeerConnection, sets remote description (await pc.setRemoteDescription(offer)), generates answer (await pc.createAnswer()), sends answer message. (4) Server forwards to Client A. (5) Client A sets remote description (await pc.setRemoteDescription(answer)). (6) Both clients generate ICE candidates (pc.onicecandidate event), send ICE messages trickle ICE. (7) Connection established via best ICE candidate (STUN direct, TURN relay). SECURITY: (1) Authenticate signaling messages - bearer token in WebSocket handshake query param, validate token on connection, reject unauthorized. (2) Prevent signaling spam - rate limit 100 messages/minute per peer_id, disconnect on violation. (3) DTLS for WebRTC data channel (automatic in WebRTC stack, encrypts media/data). (4) SDP validation - reject malformed SDP (libsdp parser), prevent buffer overflow attacks. SCALABILITY: Signaling server load - 1000 concurrent WebSocket connections = ~200MB RAM (Node.js) + ~5% CPU (message relay only, no processing). Horizontal scaling: Redis pub/sub for multi-server (servers subscribe to peer_id channels, forward messages). Example: Server1 has peer A, Server2 has peer B, A to B message goes A to Server1 to Redis to Server2 to B. 10k+ concurrent connections with 3-5 servers + Redis. FALLBACK: If signaling server unreachable, (1) Manual SDP exchange (terrible UX) - initiator copies offer to clipboard, sends via email/chat, responder pastes into app, generates answer, sends back. (2) Pre-shared connection codes - master generates invite code (encrypted peer_id+multiaddrs+auth_token), client enters code, app extracts peer_id, attempts direct connection (if LAN) or TURN relay (if internet). Connection codes expire in 5 minutes (short-lived security). MONOTERMINAL RECOMMENDATION: WebSocket signaling with bearer auth, Redis for horizontal scaling, connection codes as fallback (not manual SDP).

findings.question: Bootstrap problem: How does first client find first master - default bootstrap mechanisms, QR codes, manual entry, trust models (TOFU), zero-config scenarios
findings.answer: DEFAULT BOOTSTRAP: (1) Hardcoded STUN server - clients use stun.l.google.com:19302 (Google public STUN, 99.9% uptime) or stun1.l.google.com through stun4.l.google.com (redundancy). STUN discovers client's public IP for NAT traversal, NOT for master discovery. (2) Centralized directory - clients query monoterminal.io/api/masters?public=true for public masters, display list in UI (hostname, session count, region). User selects master, client retrieves multiaddrs, attempts connection. (3) Pre-configured endpoint - CLI flag --master https://master.example.com or config file master_url: wss://192.168.1.100:8080. QR CODE PAIRING: Master generates QR code containing JSON with peer_id, multiaddrs list, temporary auth token, expiry timestamp plus 300 seconds. Client scans QR (mobile camera, ZXing/ML Kit), extracts peer_id+multiaddrs, attempts direct connection (LAN) or signaling (internet), presents token for auth. Flow: Master shows QR on screen then Client app Add Master then Scan QR then Auto-connect (1-click, <5s). Expiry 5 minutes (short-lived security, prevents stale QR reuse). MANUAL ENTRY: Client UI has Add Master Manually with fields: (1) IP/hostname (e.g., 192.168.1.100 or master.example.com), (2) Port (default 8080), (3) Optional peer_id for verification. Client constructs multiaddr /ip4/192.168.1.100/tcp/8080, attempts connection. TRUST-ON-FIRST-USE (TOFU): On first connection, client receives master's TLS certificate or peer_id (libp2p PeerId = hash of public key). Client prompts Trust this master? Fingerprint: abc123. User accepts then client stores peer_id+fingerprint in local database. Subsequent connections verify peer_id matches, reject if mismatch (MITM detection). Similar to SSH fingerprint verification. ZERO-CONFIG (LAN): mDNS auto-discovery on same WiFi (no internet, no configuration). Client app launches then mDNS browse for _monoterminal._tcp.local then displays discovered masters then user taps to connect then TOFU prompt then done. Ideal for home/office LAN, no external dependencies. MONOTERMINAL DEFAULT HAPPY PATH: (1) Mobile: QR code primary (fastest, most user-friendly), mDNS auto-discovery secondary (same WiFi), directory tertiary (internet). (2) Desktop: mDNS auto-discovery primary (LAN), directory secondary (internet), manual entry fallback. (3) CLI: --master flag or config file (power users, scripting).

findings.question: Connection pool management: Limits and eviction policies - max connections total, per-session limits, eviction strategies, resource tracking, DoS prevention
findings.answer: LIMITS: Master enforces three-level connection limits: (1) Total connections: max_clients_total=1000 (global cap, all sessions combined), enforced at accept() - if current_clients >= 1000, close new connection with BUSY error code. (2) Per-session connections: max_clients_per_session=50 (prevent single session from monopolizing), enforced at ATTACH message - if session.clients.len() >= 50, reject with SESSION_FULL error. (3) Per-client sessions: max_sessions_per_client=10 (prevent client from attaching to too many sessions), tracked via client_id -> attached_sessions HashMap. EVICTION POLICIES: (1) Idle timeout - track last_activity timestamp per client (updated on any message received), evict if current_time - last_activity > 30min for unauthenticated, unlimited for authenticated (tmux behavior). (2) LRU eviction - when max_clients_total reached, evict oldest idle unauthenticated client first (sort by last_activity ascending, close connection gracefully with EVICTED message). (3) Priority tiers - authenticated clients have higher priority than unauthenticated, clients with active input (last_input_time < 60s) higher priority than passive viewers. (4) Graceful degradation - when approaching max (e.g., 80% capacity), log warning, optionally notify admin, prepare for eviction. RESOURCE TRACKING: (1) Memory per connection - client_struct ~1KB (metadata), write_buffer up to 1MB (scrollback sync, bounded queue), total ~1.001MB per client. 1000 clients = ~1GB RAM for connections. (2) File descriptor limit - each client = 1 fd (socket), check ulimit -n (default 1024, increase to 65536 for production via ulimit -n 65536 or systemd LimitNOFILE=65536). (3) Bandwidth per connection - typical 1-10 KB/s active usage, 0.5-2 KB/s keepalive (ping/pong), burst up to 500 KB/s during scrollback sync. 1000 clients = 500MB/s to 10GB/s theoretical max (unlikely all active simultaneously). DENIAL-OF-SERVICE PREVENTION: (1) Rate limiting - max 10 connections/minute per source IP (leaky bucket algorithm), block IP if exceeded for 10 minutes. (2) Authentication timeout - unauthenticated clients must send AUTH message within 30s or disconnect (prevent connection slot exhaustion). (3) Message rate limiting - max 100 messages/minute per client (prevent flooding master with malformed messages). (4) Slow-loris mitigation - detect clients with slow send rate (write buffer full but socket writable), disconnect after 60s stall. MONITORING: Prometheus metrics: monoterminal_connections_total{state=active|idle|unauthenticated}, monoterminal_connections_evicted_total{reason=idle|limit|banned}, monoterminal_session_clients_total{session_id}. Alert when connections > 800 (80% capacity).

findings.question: Session lifecycle: Attach, detach, resume flow - state machines, scrollback synchronization, concurrent clients support, orphaned session handling
findings.answer: ATTACH FLOW: Client connects to master (WebSocket/TCP), sends ATTACH{session_id, resume_offset?} message. Master validates: (1) Session exists (lookup in sessions HashMap), (2) Client has permission (check ACL), (3) Not exceeding max_clients_per_session. Master adds client_id to session.clients Vec, sends session metadata response: {session_id, shell_type, current_dir, rows, cols, uptime, scrollback_length}. Scrollback synchronization: (1) Full sync (default) - master sends last 10k lines from ringbuffer (~1MB, 50-200ms), client renders from top. (2) Offset-based sync - client provides resume_offset (sequence number or line index), master sends lines with seq > offset (incremental, 5-50ms). PTY output fan-out starts: master reads PTY master fd, broadcasts bytes to all session.clients via WebSocket Binary frames. Concurrent clients see identical output (synchronized scrollback + live stream). DETACH FLOW: Client sends DETACH message or closes WebSocket connection. Master removes client_id from session.clients Vec. Session persists (PTY continues running, shell alive, scrollback retained). No graceful shutdown of session unless explicitly requested via KILL_SESSION message (only session owner can kill). RESUME FLOW: Client reconnects (same or different device), sends ATTACH{session_id, last_seen_offset}. Master checks session still alive (shell process exists via kill(pid, 0)), responds with metadata + scrollback delta. If session dead (shell exited), master responds SESSION_DEAD{exit_code, exit_time}, client displays error. CONCURRENT CLIENTS: Multiple clients attached to same session simultaneously (Google Docs style collaboration). Input: all clients can send input (write to PTY master), arrives in order received (no input locking by default). Output: all clients receive identical PTY output (broadcast). Cursor position sync: optional client-side cursor broadcast {client_id, row, col}, rendered as colored rectangles (not PTY cursor). ORPHANED SESSIONS: Session with zero clients for extended period. Policies: (1) Keep forever (tmux default) - session runs indefinitely until explicit kill. (2) Auto-kill after idle timeout - if session.clients.is_empty() for >24 hours AND no PTY output for >1 hour, send SIGHUP to shell, cleanup session. (3) User preference - configurable per session via session.auto_kill_timeout. Zombie prevention: master monitors shell process via SIGCHLD handler, cleanup session immediately when shell exits (even if clients attached).

findings.question: Bandwidth optimization: Reduce mobile data usage - compression, adaptive quality, deduplication, throttling, bandwidth metrics
findings.answer: COMPRESSION: (1) zstd for scrollback sync - compress last 10k lines before sending, ~50% compression ratio (1MB -> 500KB), ~5-10ms CPU overhead (acceptable). Rust: zstd crate (zstd::encode_all). (2) Optional for live PTY stream - adds 5-10ms latency (noticeable keystroke delay), saves 30-50% bandwidth. Enable only for slow connections (<100 KB/s detected via throughput monitoring). ADAPTIVE QUALITY: (1) Low-bandwidth mode - client sends ENABLE_LOW_BANDWIDTH flag, master responds by (a) disabling ANSI colors (strip escape sequences, text-only), (b) reducing scrollback sync to 1k lines instead of 10k, (c) batching output updates (wait 100ms, send accumulated). Reduces bandwidth by 60-70%. (2) Auto-detect slow connections - master tracks per-client throughput via write buffer fill rate, if buffer >50% full for >10s, automatically enable low-bandwidth mode, send LOW_BANDWIDTH_MODE_ENABLED notification. DEDUPLICATION: PTY output is unique per keystroke (no deduplication opportunity). However, session metadata broadcast (session list updates) can be deduplicated - send only changed fields (delta encoding). Example: session_count changes 5->6, send DELTA{session_id, session_count:6} instead of full metadata. THROTTLING: (1) Limit scrollback sync bandwidth - send max 1MB/s per client, if scrollback >1MB split into chunks (1MB chunk, 1s delay, next chunk). Prevents mobile data exhaustion during large scrollback. (2) Batch small output updates - buffer PTY output for 50ms, send single WebSocket frame (reduces frame overhead, 2-14 bytes per frame). (3) Differentiated QoS - prioritize input messages (low latency critical), batch output messages (latency tolerant). METRICS: Typical bandwidth (per client): (1) Idle with keepalive - 0.5-2 KB/s (ping/pong every 30s, ~50 bytes). (2) Active typing - 5-20 KB/s (keystrokes + echo + prompt updates). (3) Scrolling output - 50-200 KB/s (tail -f log, build output). (4) Burst (git clone, npm install) - 500-2000 KB/s (sustained high output). (5) Scrollback sync (initial attach) - burst 500KB in 0.5-1s (10k lines, compressed). Mobile data usage estimates: 1 hour active development = 50-100 MB without optimization, 20-40 MB with compression+adaptive quality.

findings.question: Error handling and recovery: Network failures, crashes, edge cases - connection drops, exponential backoff, protocol errors, authentication failures, master crashes, split-brain scenarios
findings.answer: CONNECTION DROPS: Detection via (1) WebSocket close event (clean disconnect), (2) read() returns 0 bytes (TCP FIN), (3) ECONNRESET/EPIPE error (abrupt close), (4) ping timeout (no pong response within 30s). Client reconnection logic: exponential backoff with jitter - initial delay 1s, multiplier 2x, max delay 60s, jitter ±500ms (prevents thundering herd). Retry indefinitely (no max retry limit, user can manually abort). Flow: connection lost -> wait 1s -> retry -> fail -> wait 2s -> retry -> fail -> wait 4s -> ... -> wait 60s -> retry loop at 60s interval. User notification: 'Reconnecting attempt N' toast, manual 'Retry Now' button. PROTOCOL ERRORS: Malformed Protobuf decoding failure -> log error with hex dump, send ERROR{code:MALFORMED_MESSAGE, detail} response, increment error_count. If error_count > 10 within 60s, disconnect client (rate limit malformed messages, prevent exploit attempts). Invalid message type (unknown opcode) -> log, send ERROR{code:UNKNOWN_MESSAGE_TYPE}, continue processing. State machine violation (e.g., ATTACH before AUTH) -> send ERROR{code:INVALID_STATE}, close connection. AUTHENTICATION FAILURES: (1) Invalid credentials (wrong password, expired token, unknown peer_id) -> send AUTH_FAILED{reason}, allow 3 retry attempts, disconnect after 3 failures, cooldown 60s before allowing new connection from same IP. (2) Permission denied (valid auth but no access to requested session) -> send PERMISSION_DENIED{session_id, required_permission}, do NOT disconnect (client can try different session). (3) Token expiration mid-session -> send TOKEN_EXPIRED, client must re-authenticate (send new AUTH message), seamless without disconnection. MASTER CRASH: All connected clients detect connection drop (see above), auto-reconnect with exponential backoff. Session state recovery: (1) Master persisted session metadata to SQLite before crash (via SIGTERM handler or periodic checkpoint every 5min). (2) On restart, master loads sessions from database, shell PIDs likely invalid (processes dead). (3) Master cannot resurrect PTY (no process state snapshot), sessions marked DEAD. (4) Clients reconnect, receive SESSION_DEAD response, display 'Session terminated (master restarted)' error. (5) User creates new session. Alternative: systemd Restart=always for auto-restart, minimize downtime. SPLIT-BRAIN SCENARIOS: (1) Two clients with stale session_id after master restart -> both send ATTACH{session_id:old_uuid}, master responds SESSION_NOT_FOUND (session was not persisted or already cleaned up). (2) Session UUID collision (extremely unlikely with UUIDv4, 2^122 space) -> reject second session creation with CONFLICT error. (3) Client sends input to non-existent session -> master responds ERROR{code:SESSION_NOT_FOUND}, client displays 'Session no longer exists'. (4) Session dies mid-stream (shell crashes, PTY closed unexpectedly) -> master detects via SIGCHLD or PTY read() returns 0, sends SESSION_CLOSED{session_id, reason:SHELL_EXITED, exit_code} to all attached clients, cleanup session. (5) PTY hangs (unresponsive shell, infinite loop) -> master detects via write timeout (PTY master write() blocks >60s), sends SIGTERM to shell, wait 5s, escalate to SIGKILL, close PTY, cleanup session.

findings.question: Protocol format decision: Protobuf vs MessagePack vs CBOR vs JSON
findings.answer: RECOMMENDATION: Protocol Buffers (proto3). OVERHEAD: Protobuf ~10-20% (vs raw binary), MessagePack ~15-25%, CBOR ~12-22%, JSON ~100-200%. SERIALIZATION: Protobuf 100-500ns/msg (prost crate), MessagePack 80-400ns (rmp-serde), CBOR 90-450ns (serde_cbor), JSON 500-2000ns (serde_json). SCHEMA EVOLUTION: Protobuf EXCELLENT (field numbers, optional/required, oneof, reserved fields, proto2→proto3 migration), MessagePack NONE (schema-less, no versioning), CBOR LIMITED (CDDL schema optional, poor tooling), JSON MANUAL (client-side validation). TOOLING: Protobuf 30+ languages (protoc, prost for Rust, grpc-web for Web), MessagePack 50+ (worse mobile support), CBOR 20+, JSON universal. VERDICT: Protobuf for MONOTERMINAL - schema evolution critical for desktop↔mobile compatibility, language support (Rust/Swift/Kotlin/TypeScript), WebRTC DataChannel compatibility (binary-first), <1% overhead vs MessagePack not worth losing schema guarantees. Per D1.5: WebSocket Protobuf framing already chosen.
sources: Terminal protocol analysis (WezTerm binary protocol, tmux control mode)

findings.question: Protocol specification: Message structure and framing
findings.answer: FRAMING (WebSocket Binary): 1 WebSocket binary frame = 1 Protobuf message (NO length prefix needed, WebSocket provides framing per RFC 6455 §5.2). ALTERNATIVE: Length-prefix (u32 big-endian + message) for raw TCP/DataChannel if WebSocket not available. HEADER: message MonoterminalMessage { string message_id = 1; // UUID v4 for request/response correlation, MessageType type = 2; // enum ATTACH=1, DETACH=2, INPUT=3, OUTPUT=4, RESIZE=5, ERROR=6..., Version version = 3; // major=u8, minor=u8, patch=u8 (semantic versioning), oneof payload { AttachRequest attach = 10; DetachRequest detach = 11; InputMessage input = 12; OutputMessage output = 13; ResizeMessage resize = 14; ErrorMessage error = 15; SessionListRequest list_sessions = 16; ... } }. SIZE LIMITS: Max 10MB for SCROLLBACK (attach sync), 64KB for INPUT (terminal input line), 1MB for OUTPUT (batch), UNLIMITED for file transfer (chunked). Per D1.5: unified session router handles message_id correlation.

findings.question: Version negotiation: Handshake protocol and compatibility
findings.answer: HANDSHAKE: Client sends HELLO{version: {major: 1, minor: 0, patch: 0}, capabilities: [COMPRESSION_ZSTD, ENCRYPTION_TLS13, FILE_TRANSFER, CLIPBOARD_SYNC]} → Server responds VERSION_OK{server_version, negotiated_capabilities} OR INCOMPATIBLE{reason, min_version_required}. SEMANTIC VERSIONING: Major (breaking protocol changes, incompatible), Minor (backward-compatible additions like new message types), Patch (bug fixes, no protocol changes). BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY: Server supports N-1 major versions (e.g., v2 server handles v1 clients by downgrading features), client must support server's major version OR upgrade. UPGRADE PATH: Server sends UPGRADE_AVAILABLE{new_version, download_url, breaking_changes: bool} on connect if client outdated, client decides (auto-update for patch/minor if breaking_changes=false, user prompt for major). FEATURE NEGOTIATION: Capabilities bitmap (COMPRESSION_ZSTD=1, COMPRESSION_GZIP=2, ENCRYPTION_TLS13=4, FILE_TRANSFER=8, CLIPBOARD_SYNC=16, P2P_WEBRTC=32 per D3.1), client/server intersect (negotiated_capabilities = client_caps & server_caps). Per D3.4: protocol error handling enforces version check before allowing messages.

findings.question: Error handling: Protocol-level error codes and recovery
findings.answer: ERROR TYPES: INVALID_MESSAGE (1, malformed Protobuf), AUTH_REQUIRED (2, unauthenticated), SESSION_NOT_FOUND (3, session ID invalid), PERMISSION_DENIED (4, unauthorized action), RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (5, >100 msgs/min per D3.4), INTERNAL_ERROR (6, server fault), PROTOCOL_VERSION_MISMATCH (7, incompatible versions). ERROR CODES: HTTP-style (4xx client errors: 400=INVALID_MESSAGE, 401=AUTH_REQUIRED, 403=PERMISSION_DENIED, 404=SESSION_NOT_FOUND, 429=RATE_LIMIT; 5xx server errors: 500=INTERNAL_ERROR, 503=SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE). ERROR RESPONSES: message ErrorMessage { uint32 code = 1; // HTTP-style, string message = 2; // human-readable, optional uint32 retry_after_seconds = 3; // for 429/503, optional string request_id = 4; // correlate to triggering message_id }. RECOVERY: Retryable (503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE → exponential backoff 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s max 60s; 429 RATE_LIMIT → wait retry_after_seconds), Fatal (401 UNAUTHORIZED → close connection, re-auth required; 400 INVALID_MESSAGE → log error, drop message). CLIENT BEHAVIOR: Log all errors locally (structured logging with request_id), show user notification for fatal errors (401, 403), auto-retry for transient (503, 429 with backoff), drop & warn for malformed (400). Per D3.4: message rate limits 100/min enforced at protocol layer.
sources: Matrix D3.4 (rate limits 100/min, protocol error handling)

findings.question: I/O streaming messages: Input, output, signals
findings.answer: INPUT: message InputMessage { string session_id = 1; bytes data = 2; // UTF-8 input, max 64KB per D4.1 } → forwards to PTY stdin (write(pty_fd, data)), NO response (fire-and-forget), client relies on WebSocket backpressure (RFC 6455 flow control). OUTPUT: message OutputMessage { string session_id = 1; bytes data = 2; // PTY stdout/stderr (binary-safe, NOT UTF-8 guaranteed), uint64 sequence = 3; // monotonic sequence number for ordering (handle out-of-order WebSocket delivery) } → broadcast to all attached clients. SIGNAL: message SignalMessage { string session_id = 1; Signal signal = 2; // enum SIGINT=2, SIGTERM=15, SIGKILL=9, SIGSTOP=19, SIGCONT=18 } → kill(pty_pid, signal), no response. FLOW CONTROL: NO per-message ACK for INPUT (WebSocket provides TCP backpressure), client buffers if WebSocket send queue full. OUTPUT sequence numbers detect gaps (missed messages, out-of-order delivery if multiple paths), client requests RESEND{start_seq, end_seq} if gap detected. BATCHING: Master batches multiple OUTPUTs into single message (100ms window OR 64KB size limit, whichever first) to reduce WebSocket frame overhead (per D4.2.4 compression optimization). findings.question: Compression and optimization: When to compress, what algorithm
findings.answer: COMPRESSION CANDIDATES: OUTPUT (scrollback, build logs, repeated text), SCROLLBACK (attach sync, 10MB limit per D4.1), FILE_TRANSFER (NOT terminal I/O, separate feature). ALGORITHM: zstd RECOMMENDED (50% ratio on text, 5-10ms latency for 64KB, streaming mode via zstd-sys crate, level 3 default), gzip FALLBACK (40% ratio, slower 15-20ms, higher CPU, zlib crate), NONE for control messages (CREATE_SESSION, RESIZE <1KB overhead not worth compression). STREAMING: zstd streaming API for incremental compression (zstd::stream::Encoder, feed data chunks, flush on 100ms window or 64KB, don't buffer full message), critical for large scrollback (10MB) to avoid memory spikes. COMPRESSION RATIO BENCHMARKS: Terminal output (ANSI escape codes, build logs) ~50-60% with zstd, ~40-50% with gzip. Example: 64KB PTY output → 32KB zstd (50%), 26KB gzip (40%), zstd faster (5-10ms vs 15-20ms gzip).

findings.question: Output buffering strategy: Server-side PTY output buffering, flush triggers, Nagle-like algorithm, interactive detection
findings.answer: BUFFER SIZE: 4KB default (typical), 16KB max (for high throughput), 64B min (interactive shell prompts). FLUSH TRIGGERS: (1) Time-based: 100ms window (balance latency vs throughput, tmux uses 10ms for low-latency mode), (2) Size-based: 4KB threshold (one WebSocket frame, avoid fragmentation), (3) Newline-based: immediate flush on '\n' if last 256 bytes contains shell prompt patterns (PS1 detection: '$ ', '> ', '# ', '% '). NAGLE-LIKE BATCHING: Combine multiple small PTY reads (10x 10B writes) → 1x 100B WebSocket frame to reduce frame overhead (2-14 bytes per frame per RFC 6455). INTERACTIVE MODE DETECTION: Heuristic: If PTY emits <50B in 10ms window AND ends with prompt pattern → immediate flush (<10ms latency). ELSE (build logs, cat, vim) → batch until 4KB OR 100ms. IMPLEMENTATION: ring buffer (circular buffer, lock-free SPSC queue via crossbeam-channel), write from PTY → buffer, flush thread checks triggers every 10ms OR on buffer threshold. TRADEOFF: Interactive latency (<10ms flush) vs throughput (4KB batching saves ~3-5% WebSocket overhead, ~50% CPU for fewer syscalls). Per D4.2.2: OUTPUT batches into single message (100ms OR 64KB).

findings.question: Flow control and backpressure: WebSocket backpressure detection, client ACK, slow client handling, buffer overflow policy
findings.answer: WEBSOCKET BACKPRESSURE DETECTION: Monitor send() result: EWOULDBLOCK (POSIX) or WouldBlock (Rust tungstenite) indicates client socket buffer full (TCP send buffer ~64KB-256KB per connection). TRACK: per-client send queue depth (max 1MB buffered per client, if exceeded → slow client mitigation). CLIENT-SIDE ACK: NO per-message acknowledgment (adds RTT latency, WebSocket provides TCP-level reliability). Instead: sequence numbers on OUTPUT (per D4.2.2) allow gap detection, client requests RESEND if gap found. SLOW CLIENT HANDLING: (1) Pause PTY reads when ALL clients' send queues >512KB (global backpressure, SIGSTOP PTY process to stop output), (2) Resume when queues drain <256KB (SIGCONT), (3) Disconnect client if queue >1MB for >30s (force disconnect, prevent memory exhaustion), (4) Show 'slow client' warning to other clients. BUFFER OVERFLOW: Server enforces 1MB per-client limit, 10MB total scrollback limit (per D4.1.2), if exceeded → drop oldest OUTPUT messages (lossy, acceptable for terminal streaming since scrollback covers history), log warning. CAN WE AFFORD LOSSY OUTPUT? YES for live streaming (scrollback provides history recovery), NO for command execution (INPUT must be reliable, WebSocket TCP guarantees). ALTERNATIVE: Drop frames for non-interactive (vim screen refresh tolerable), NEVER drop for shell output (command results critical). Per D3.4: message rate limits 100/min prevent client DOS.

findings.question: Multi-client synchronization: Output fan-out, client offset tracking, resync mechanism, input arbitration, conflict resolution
findings.answer: OUTPUT FAN-OUT: Server broadcasts same OUTPUT message to all attached clients (1→N, iterate client list, tungstenite::send() to each WebSocket). OPTIMIZATION: Share Protobuf-encoded buffer across clients (serialize once, send N times, saves CPU ~40-60% vs per-client serialization). CLIENT OFFSET TRACKING: Each client tracks its own sequence number (stored in client state: last_received_sequence), server includes sequence in OUTPUT (monotonic counter, per-session, starts at 0, increments per message). RESYNC MECHANISM: Client detects gap (received sequence 105, expected 103 → gap of 2 messages 103-104), sends RESEND{session_id, start_seq: 103, end_seq: 104}, server retrieves from scrollback buffer (if available, else returns ERROR 'sequence expired, ATTACH to re-sync'). FALLBACK: If gap >1000 messages OR scrollback expired → client does full ATTACH (re-download entire scrollback, per D4.2.1, max 10MB). INPUT ARBITRATION: All clients' INPUT merged FIFO (first-come-first-served based on server receive timestamp), NO priority system (collaborative session, all clients equal). LOCK-STEP: Server forwards INPUT to PTY in receive order, all clients see same OUTPUT sequence. CONFLICT RESOLUTION: Two clients type simultaneously → server receives in network order (TCP guarantees ordering per connection), timestamps resolve ties (server_receive_timestamp_ns), PTY processes inputs sequentially. NO conflict (terminal input is sequential by nature, unlike collaborative editing). Per D1.5: unified session router handles multi-client fan-out.

findings.question: Round-trip time minimization: Target RTT, WebSocket ping/pong, TCP_NODELAY (disable Nagle), zero-copy paths, minimum achievable RTT benchmarks
findings.answer: TARGET RTT: <50ms LAN (local network, same subnet), <150ms internet (US coast-to-coast, London-NYC ~80ms), <300ms intercontinental (US-Europe ~100-150ms, US-Asia ~150-250ms). WEBSOCKET PING/PONG: Send PING every 30s (RFC 6455 §5.5.2, keepalive + measure RTT), client measures RTT = (pong_received_timestamp - ping_sent_timestamp), server tracks per-client RTT history (rolling average, 10 samples). TCP_NODELAY: ENABLE (disable Nagle's algorithm, setsockopt TCP_NODELAY=1) for WebSocket connections to prevent 40-200ms delay from Nagle batching (Nagle waits for ACK before sending small packets, terrible for interactive terminal). ZERO-COPY PATHS: Linux: splice() for PTY→socket (kernel-space transfer, avoid user-space copy, ~30% CPU reduction), sendfile() for scrollback file→socket, io_uring for async I/O (reduce syscall overhead). Rust: tokio::io::copy() uses zero-copy when available, tungstenite::WebSocket::write_frame() with BytesMut avoids allocations. MINIMUM ACHIEVABLE RTT BENCHMARKS: Local PTY (echo test): 1-5ms (PTY read/write syscalls), WebSocket local (127.0.0.1): 5-15ms (WebSocket framing + TCP loopback), LAN (same subnet): 10-30ms (network switch latency 1-5ms), Internet (50ms ping): 50-100ms (network latency dominates), Intercontinental (150ms ping): 150-300ms. MEASUREMENT: Continuous RTT tracking via PING/PONG (30s interval), percentiles (p50, p95, p99), alert if p95 >300ms (degraded network). Per D3.1: WebRTC data channels 10-300ms latency.

findings.question: Network condition adaptation: Adaptive batching based on latency, compression threshold tuning, quality degradation on packet loss/high latency, continuous measurement
findings.answer: ADAPTIVE BATCHING: Measure RTT continuously (WebSocket PING/PONG every 30s), adjust flush window: High latency (>200ms) → batch aggressively (200ms window, accumulate more output to amortize RTT), Low latency (<50ms) → flush faster (50ms window, prioritize interactive responsiveness). FORMULA: flush_window_ms = clamp(RTT_p95 * 1.5, 50ms, 200ms). COMPRESSION THRESHOLD: High latency OR low bandwidth (RTT >200ms OR throughput <1Mbps) → compress earlier (2KB threshold vs 4KB default), Fast network (RTT <50ms AND throughput >10Mbps) → compress only large payloads (16KB threshold, avoid CPU overhead for small messages). BANDWIDTH DETECTION: Measure throughput (bytes sent / time elapsed over 10s window), classify: Slow (<1Mbps), Medium (1-10Mbps), Fast (>10Mbps). QUALITY DEGRADATION: On packet loss (detect via sequence number gaps, >5 gaps/min) OR high latency (RTT p95 >500ms for 3 consecutive samples), reduce features: (1) Disable scrollback sync on ATTACH (send only last 1k lines vs 10k), (2) Throttle output to 10 FPS (batch outputs, send every 100ms max, reduce WebSocket frame rate), (3) Disable live cursor position updates (send only on key commands, not every keystroke), (4) Reduce PING interval to 60s (save bandwidth). MEASUREMENT: Continuous monitoring: RTT (PING/PONG), throughput (bytes/s), packet loss (sequence gaps), store last 60s history, percentiles (p50, p95, p99). AUTO-RECOVERY: When network improves (RTT p95 <200ms for 30s), restore full features. Per D3.4: adaptive compression based on network conditions.

findings.question: Client-side rendering optimization: Local echo, predictive rendering, dirty region tracking, frame rate limiting, safety of local echo
findings.answer: LOCAL ECHO: Client shows typed characters immediately (optimistic UI, append to terminal buffer before server echoes), server echoes back (if mismatch → correction, overwrite client prediction with server truth). SAFETY: Generally safe for printable ASCII (a-z, 0-9, space), UNSAFE for: (1) Control characters (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z → client doesn't know if server will intercept), (2) Shell with custom echo handling (stty -echo, password prompts hide input), (3) Applications like vim (input triggers commands, not echoes). HEURISTIC: Enable local echo only in 'shell mode' (detected by prompt pattern, PS1), disable in 'application mode' (vim, less, htop detected by TERM environment or escape sequences). PREDICTIVE RENDERING: Client predicts cursor position during typing (advance cursor by 1 column per character, word wrap at terminal width), server confirms or corrects (if server cursor differs → snap to server position, show brief 'correcting' indicator). DIRTY REGION TRACKING: Render only changed terminal cells (xterm.js does this automatically via diff algorithm, WebGL terminal needs manual implementation), track dirty rectangles (x1, y1, x2, y2), redraw only dirty regions (~50-80% GPU savings vs full-screen redraw). FRAME RATE LIMITING: Cap rendering at 60 FPS (or device refresh rate, requestAnimationFrame), don't render every OUTPUT message (if 10 OUTPUTs arrive in 16ms → accumulate, render once at vsync), prevents GPU thrashing on high-frequency updates (build logs, yes flood). TRADEOFF: Local echo reduces perceived latency (typing feels instant) but risks correction flicker (user sees wrong character briefly, then corrected). Per D2.3: xterm.js expects sequential output for VT100 rendering.

findings.question: Protocol overhead measurement: Protobuf wire format overhead, WebSocket framing bytes, total overhead calculation, compression effectiveness benchmarks, typical session analysis
findings.answer: PROTOBUF OVERHEAD: Wire format adds ~10-20 bytes per message: (1) Field tags (varint, 1-5 bytes per field, e.g., field 1 = 1 byte, field 16 = 2 bytes), (2) Length prefixes (varint for bytes/string fields, 1-5 bytes for <128B, 2 bytes for 128B-16KB), (3) Message framing (WebSocket provides framing, NO additional length prefix needed per D4.1.2). EXAMPLE: OutputMessage { session_id (36B UUID string) + data (100B) + sequence (u64) } → Protobuf: field tags ~3B + length prefixes ~2B + data 136B = 141B total (5B overhead, 3.5%). WEBSOCKET FRAMING: RFC 6455 §5.2: (1) Header: 2 bytes (FIN + opcode + mask bit + payload length 0-125), (2) Extended payload length: +2 bytes (126-65535), +8 bytes (>65535), (3) Masking key: 4 bytes (client→server only, server→client NO mask), (4) Payload: actual data. CLIENT→SERVER (masked): 2 (header) + 2 (extended length for >125B) + 4 (mask) = 8 bytes overhead. SERVER→CLIENT (unmasked): 2 (header) + 2 (extended length) = 4 bytes overhead. TOTAL OVERHEAD (100B PTY output → WebSocket): Protobuf 5B (3.5%) + WebSocket 4B (server→client) = 9B overhead on 105B = 8.6% total. For 1KB output: Protobuf 10B (1%) + WebSocket 4B (0.4%) = 14B overhead = 1.4% total. COMPRESSION EFFECTIVENESS: Typical shell session (ls, vim, npm build): zstd ~40-60% reduction. BENCHMARK: (a) cat large file (100KB text): zstd 55% (45KB compressed), overhead: Protobuf 15B + WebSocket 4B = 19B on 45KB = 0.04% (negligible). (b) vim editing (ANSI escape codes, cursor moves): zstd 45% (high escape code redundancy), overhead: Protobuf 8B + WebSocket 4B = 12B per frame, ~5-10% (many small frames). (c) npm build output (1MB logs, repeated patterns): zstd 60% (400KB compressed), overhead: Protobuf 20B + WebSocket 6B = 26B on 400KB = 0.006% (negligible). BYTES/SECOND REAL-WORLD: (a) cat large file: 500KB/s uncompressed → 225KB/s compressed (zstd), ~2Mbps. (b) vim editing: 5-10KB/s (interactive, low volume). (c) npm build: 200KB/s average, spikes to 1MB/s (parallel compiler output). Per D4.2.4: zstd 50% ratio on terminal output.

findings.question: TLS configuration for WebSocket server: versions, cipher suites, certificates, rotation, performance
findings.answer:
**TLS Version:** TLS 1.3 only (RFC 8446) for new deployments, with fallback to TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) for compatibility if needed. TLS 1.3 reduces handshake to 1-RTT (vs 2-RTT in 1.2), eliminating 50-100ms latency. Deprecate TLS 1.0/1.1 (IETF RFC 8996).

**Cipher Suites (TLS 1.3):** Mandatory support for TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (AEAD ciphers with perfect forward secrecy). Add TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 for mobile clients (better ARM performance, no AES-NI required). TLS 1.3 removed weak ciphers; all suites provide PFS via ECDHE.

**Certificate Sources:**
- Self-signed: TOFU (trust-on-first-use) model, pin certificate fingerprint on first connect. Generate with 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit ECDSA (P-256). Store in ~/.monoterminal/known_hosts.
- Let's Encrypt: Free automated certs via ACME protocol (RFC 8555). Requires public domain, HTTP-01 or DNS-01 challenge. Use certbot or acme-client.
- User-provided CA: Corporate environments with internal CA. Import root cert to client trust stores.

**Certificate Rotation:**
- Self-signed: 90-day validity (industry standard, limits exposure window). Auto-rotate 7 days before expiry, notify clients to re-pin.
- Let's Encrypt: 90-day validity, auto-renew at 60 days via ACME. Use certbot timers or systemd service.
- CA-issued: 1-year max (CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements). Track expiry in database, alert 30 days before.

**Performance Impact:**
- TLS 1.3 handshake: 50-100ms (1-RTT vs 100-200ms for TLS 1.2 2-RTT). 0-RTT resumption reduces to <10ms.
- AES-GCM throughput: ~5-10% CPU overhead on modern x86 with AES-NI. Without AES-NI (ARM), ChaCha20-Poly1305 is 2-3x faster.
- Memory: ~40KB per connection for TLS buffers (rustls), ~60KB for OpenSSL.
- Terminal streaming: negligible impact at <100Mbps (typical terminal bandwidth). Encryption adds <1ms latency per frame.

findings.question: Certificate pinning for P2P: storage, format, verification, rotation, attack scenarios
findings.answer:
**Pin Storage:**
- SQLite database: pins table with columns (peer_id, cert_hash, pinned_at, last_seen).
- File-based: ~/.monoterminal/known_peers (SSH-style format): peer_id SHA256:abc123... 2026-08-14T10:00:00Z
- Recommendation: SQLite for structured queries (list all pins, filter by date), file for simplicity and inspectability.

**Pin Format:**
- SHA256 hash of SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) - 32 bytes, hex-encoded (64 chars).
- Format: SHA256: prefix + base64 or hex (consistent with SSH fingerprints).
- Example: SHA256:6kxKFQ7qQpP8A3VjjJ3vW5ZK5L0tZxE1xQn8r2c3D4=
- Do NOT pin full certificate (changes on renewal); pin public key only.

**Pin Verification:**
- On WebRTC connection (after DTLS handshake), extract peer certificate.
- Compute SHA256(SPKI) and compare to stored pin.
- If match: proceed. If mismatch: DISCONNECT + show MITM warning dialog.
- If no pin exists: TOFU mode - store pin and mark as first connect (user should verify via out-of-band channel).

**Pin Rotation:**
- Challenge: Master rotates certificate (90-day cycle) but clients have old pin.
- Solution 1: Re-pairing via QR code (user scans new QR, updates pin).
- Solution 2: Signed cert update message (master signs new cert with old private key, client verifies signature, updates pin).
- Solution 3: Grace period (accept old + new cert for 7 days during rotation).
- Recommendation: Solution 2 for automated rotation, Solution 1 as fallback.

**Attack Scenarios:**
- MITM on first connect: Attacker intercepts initial pairing, pins their certificate. Mitigation: require physical access to scan QR (attacker needs proximity).
- Certificate substitution: Attacker replaces master's cert during rotation. Mitigation: signed update messages + user confirmation for unexpected changes.
- Pin deletion attack: Attacker wipes client's pin database, triggers re-pin. Mitigation: protect pin storage with OS keychain (iOS Keychain, Android KeyStore).

findings.question: End-to-end encryption for sensitive sessions: use case, key exchange, encryption, key management, trade-offs
findings.answer:
**Use Case:**
- Protect against compromised relay server (WebSocket proxy cannot decrypt).
- Bypass corporate TLS inspection (corporate proxy sees only encrypted payload).
- Zero-trust environments (do not trust network layer, end-to-end verification).
- Compliance: healthcare (HIPAA), finance (PCI-DSS) requiring end-to-end encryption.
- Target: government, enterprise, security-conscious users.

**Key Exchange:**
- Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) with X25519 curve (Curve25519, 128-bit security).
- Client generates ephemeral keypair (32-byte private key, 32-byte public key, ~50μs on modern CPU).
- Exchange: CLIENT_HELLO{client_pubkey} → SERVER_HELLO{server_pubkey}.
- Shared secret: scalar multiplication of client_privkey × server_pubkey = 32-byte shared secret.
- Derive session key: HKDF-SHA256(shared_secret, salt) → 32-byte AES-256 key or ChaCha20 key.

**Encryption:**
- ChaCha20-Poly1305: stream cipher + MAC, optimized for software (no AES-NI needed), constant-time (side-channel resistant).
- Throughput: ~1-2 GB/s on modern CPU, ~500 MB/s on ARM.
- AES-256-GCM: block cipher + MAC, hardware-accelerated on x86 (AES-NI), provides authenticated encryption.
- Nonce: 96-bit (12-byte) random nonce per message, never reuse (critical for GCM security).
- Frame format: [nonce 12B][ciphertext N bytes][tag 16B].

**Key Management:**
- Ephemeral session keys: generate new keypair per ATTACH operation (perfect forward secrecy).
- Key lifetime: session duration only, discard on DETACH.
- No long-lived keys (reduce exposure window).
- Optional: long-lived identity keys (Ed25519) for authentication + ephemeral session keys for encryption (Signal Protocol pattern).

**Trade-offs:**
- Latency: +20-50ms (key exchange + encryption overhead per frame).
- CPU: doubles encryption cost (TLS + E2EE), ~10-15% total CPU overhead.
- Complexity: key rotation, nonce management, debugging (cannot inspect encrypted frames).
- Battery: mobile clients see 5-10% battery drain increase.
- Recommendation: OPTIONAL flag (--e2ee), default OFF for simplicity, enable for high-security use cases.

**rustls (Pure Rust TLS):**
- Pros: Memory-safe (no buffer overflows, use-after-free), no OpenSSL dependency (reproducible builds), TLS 1.3 native support, small binary size (~100KB increase).
- Cons: Newer library (less battle-tested than OpenSSL), no FIPS 140-2 certification (yet).
- Performance: Handshake 80-120ms (1-RTT TLS 1.3), throughput ~3-4 GB/s AES-GCM, ~1-2 GB/s ChaCha20-Poly1305.
- Benchmarks (rustls 0.21+): ~95% of OpenSSL throughput, competitive handshake times.
- Use case: Default choice for memory safety, reproducible builds, no system dependencies.

**openssl-sys (OpenSSL Bindings):**
- Pros: Battle-tested (30+ years), FIPS 140-2 modules available (OpenSSL 3.0+), security patches via system updates, broad cipher suite support.
- Cons: Unsafe Rust bindings (potential for memory bugs), system dependency (complicates cross-compilation), CVE exposure via system OpenSSL.
- Performance: Handshake 70-100ms, throughput ~4-5 GB/s AES-GCM (baseline reference).
- FIPS compliance: OpenSSL 3.0 FIPS module (CMVP certificate #4282), required for government/defense.
- Use case: FIPS compliance required, legacy system integration, maximum compatibility.

**native-tls (Platform TLS):**
- Pros: Platform integration (SChannel on Windows, Secure Transport on macOS, OpenSSL on Linux), system trust stores (no manual cert management), OS security updates.
- Cons: Inconsistent API across platforms, debugging complexity (different TLS stacks), no direct cipher suite control.
- Performance: Varies by platform (Windows ~90-110ms handshake, macOS ~80-100ms, Linux = OpenSSL).
- Use case: Desktop apps needing system integration, trust store compatibility.

**Decision Matrix:**
- Memory safety priority: rustls (eliminates entire class of CVEs).
- FIPS compliance required: openssl-sys with FIPS module.
- Platform integration (desktop GUI): native-tls.
- Cross-platform CLI/server: rustls (consistent behavior, no system deps).
- Mobile (iOS/Android): native-tls for platform trust stores.

**Recommendation for MONOTERMINAL:**
- Master terminal (server): rustls (memory safety, no CVEs via C deps, reproducible builds).
- Desktop client: native-tls (system trust stores for Let's Encrypt certs).
- Mobile client: native-tls (platform keychain integration).
- Enterprise variant: openssl-sys with FIPS module (government/compliance use case).

findings.question: Client authentication mechanisms: SSH keys, password+TOTP, certificates, tokens, mobile-specific
findings.answer:
**SSH Key-Based (Primary):**
- Ed25519 keys (32-byte public key, 64-byte signature, ~50μs sign/verify, 128-bit security).
- Client workflow: generate keypair, send public key to master, store in authorized_keys.
- Authentication: Client signs challenge with private key, master verifies with stored public key.
- Advantages: no password transmission, phishing-resistant, hardware key support (YubiKey via OpenSSH).

**Password + TOTP (Fallback):**
- Password: bcrypt hash (cost factor 12-14, ~200-500ms to verify, resistant to brute force).
- TOTP (RFC 6238): 6-digit code, 30-second window, HMAC-SHA1.
- Enrollment: master generates TOTP secret (160-bit random), client scans QR code.
- Verification: client sends {username, password, totp_code}, master verifies both within ±1 time step (90-second window for clock drift).
- Backup codes: 8x 8-digit codes (hashed with bcrypt), use once for account recovery.

**Certificate-Based (mTLS):**
- Mutual TLS: client presents X.509 certificate during TLS handshake, master verifies signature against CA public key.
- Certificate structure: subject = client_id, issuer = master CA, validity 1 year, key usage = digitalSignature.
- Enrollment: master generates CA keypair, signs client cert request (CSR), client stores cert + private key.
- Use case: enterprise environments with PKI infrastructure.

**Token-Based (JWT):**
- Issued AFTER initial authentication (SSH/password/cert), used for subsequent requests.
- 15-min access token, 30-day refresh token (see Q4 for full lifecycle).

**Mobile-Specific:**
- Biometric unlock: FaceID (iOS), TouchID (iOS/macOS), Android BiometricPrompt API.
- Workflow: private key stored in Keychain (iOS) or KeyStore (Android), encrypted with biometric key.
- Unlock triggers biometric prompt → decrypt private key → sign challenge.
- Fallback: device PIN/password if biometric fails.

findings.question: Authorization model: RBAC, session ownership, permissions, revocation
findings.answer:
**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC):**
- Roles: admin (all sessions, system config), user (own sessions only), read-only (attach but no input/control).
- Permissions: admin (full), user (own sessions), read-only (attach shared sessions, no input).

**Session Ownership:**
- Creator is owner: user who sends SESSION_CREATE becomes owner.
- Owner privileges: SESSION_CLOSE (terminate), SESSION_KILL (force-kill process), GRANT_ACCESS (share), REVOKE_ACCESS (kick clients).
- Non-owner: can ATTACH if granted access, cannot CLOSE (only DETACH).
- Orphaned sessions: if owner disconnects, session persists until explicit CLOSE or master restart (configurable: auto-close after 24h).

**Permission Storage:**
- SQLite schema: session_permissions table with (session_id, user_id, role, granted_at, granted_by).
- Check on every SESSION_CONTROL message: query for permission, cache in memory HashMap.
- Cache invalidation on GRANT/REVOKE.

**Default Policy:**
- New session: creator gets owner role, no other users have access.
- Sharing: owner sends GRANT_ACCESS → master inserts into session_permissions → broadcasts SESSION_SHARED to all clients.
- Joining: client sends SESSION_ATTACH → master checks permissions → if granted, establish data channel; if denied, return ERROR.

**Revocation:**
- Owner revocation: REVOKE_ACCESS → master removes from session_permissions → sends SESSION_DETACH to kicked client → closes WebSocket.
- Admin revocation: admin can revoke any access (override owner).
- Grace period: 30-second warning before disconnect.
findings.data_quality: authoritative - based on NIST RBAC and industry best practices

findings.question: Pairing security for mobile clients: QR content, protocol, replay protection, attestation, attacks
findings.answer:
**QR Code Content (~180 bytes):**
- Version byte: 0x01 (protocol version).
- Ed25519 public key: 32 bytes (master's long-term identity key).
- Master IP: 4 bytes (IPv4) or 16 bytes (IPv6) + 2 bytes port.
- Certificate fingerprint: SHA256 of master's TLS cert (32 bytes).
- Timestamp: 8 bytes (Unix timestamp, for expiry check).
- Nonce: 16 bytes (random, prevents QR reuse).
- Signature: 64 bytes (Ed25519 signature of all above fields).
- Encoding: Base64, URL: monoterminal://pair?data=<base64>.

**Pairing Protocol:**
1. Master displays QR code (refreshes every 5 minutes).
2. Client scans QR → validates signature → checks timestamp (within 5 minutes).
3. Client generates ephemeral Ed25519 keypair.
4. Client → Master: PAIR_REQUEST{client_pubkey, device_name, qr_nonce} over TLS.
5. Master verifies qr_nonce matches displayed QR, checks timestamp.
6. Master → Client: PAIR_ACCEPT{master_pubkey, session_token (JWT, 24-hour expiry)}.
7. Client stores: master_pubkey, session_token, cert_fingerprint.
8. Master stores: client_pubkey in authorized_keys, device_name, paired_at.

**Replay Protection:**
- QR nonce: 16-byte random, included in QR and signed. Master maintains nonce_cache (LRU, 1000 entries). Reject if nonce reused.
- Timestamp: 5-minute expiry window. Reject if outside window.
- One-time use: QR expires after successful pairing.

**Attestation (Trust Model):**
- Physical proximity: user must physically access master's terminal to see QR (defeats remote attacks).
- Visual verification: client displays master fingerprint (first 8 hex chars), user confirms it matches master's screen.
- TOFU model: trust on first use, subsequent connections verify against pinned pubkey.

**Attack Scenarios:**
1. QR phishing: Attacker shows fake QR. Mitigation: user verifies master's screen location, fingerprint confirmation.
2. Shoulder surfing: Attacker photographs QR. Mitigation: 5-minute expiry, one-time nonce, TLS prevents reuse.
3. MITM on pairing: Attacker intercepts PAIR_REQUEST. Mitigation: TLS cert pinning, Ed25519 signature on QR.
4. Replay attack: Attacker reuses old QR. Mitigation: timestamp + nonce.
sources: RFC 8709 - Ed25519 for public key cryptography
Signal Protocol pairing (safety numbers for verification)
WhatsApp Web pairing QR code design
OWASP Mobile Security Testing Guide - Pairing mechanisms

findings.question: Session token lifecycle: JWT format, expiry, refresh flow, revocation, storage
findings.answer:
**JWT Format (RFC 7519):**
- Header: {alg: EdDSA, typ: JWT} (Ed25519 signatures).
- Payload: {iss: monoterminal-master, sub: user_id, aud: monoterminal-client, exp: 15min, iat, nbf, jti: unique-token-id, session_id, role}.
- Signature: Ed25519(header + payload, master_privkey) → 64 bytes.
- Encoded: ~250 bytes total.

**Token Expiry:**
- Access token: 15 minutes (OWASP recommendation).
- Refresh token: 30 days (long-lived, revocable).
- Rationale: short access token limits exposure, long refresh token reduces re-auth friction.

**Refresh Flow:**
1. Client detects access token expiry or receives 401 Unauthorized.
2. Client → Master: REFRESH_TOKEN{refresh_token} over TLS.
3. Master verifies: signature, checks revoked_tokens table, validates exp.
4. If valid: generate new access_token, optionally new refresh_token (refresh token rotation).
5. Master → Client: {access_token, refresh_token (if rotated)}.
6. Client stores new tokens, retries original request.

**Revocation:**
- Challenge: JWTs are stateless (master doesn't track issued tokens).
- Solution: Revoked tokens table (SQLite): (jti, revoked_at, reason, expires_at).
- On verification: master checks revoked_tokens table (fast, indexed).
- Revocation triggers: logout, password change, device de-pairing, admin action.
- Cleanup: periodic job removes expired tokens.

**Secure Storage:**
- iOS: Keychain (kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly).
- Android: EncryptedSharedPreferences (AES-256-GCM, key in KeyStore).
- Desktop: OS credential store (Keychain/Credential Manager/libsecret).
- Fallback: Encrypted file (AES-256-GCM, key via PBKDF2, 100k iterations).
- Never: LocalStorage, plain text, logs.
sources: OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet

findings.question: Attack surface analysis for MONOTERMINAL
findings.answer: 6 primary attack vectors: (1) Network: MITM on WebSocket/WebRTC, relay eavesdropping, DNS poisoning; (2) Auth bypass: SSH key brute force (rate limit 5/hour), stolen JWT (15min expiry), QR MITM, cookie theft; (3) Authz escalation: read-only→write via session hijacking, privilege escalation; (4) DoS: connection flood (100/min), message flood (100/min), scrollback exhaustion (100MB/session), compression bombs (10:1 limit), PTY fork bomb (1000 proc/session); (5) Data exfiltration: scrollback theft (encrypted at rest), admin recording (logged), clipboard sniffing, env var leakage (filter AWS_*, *_TOKEN); (6) Supply chain: malicious crate (cargo audit/deny), compromised binary (code signing), typosquatting. Rate limits: 100 conn/min/IP, 100 msg/min/client, 5 auth/hour. Quotas: 10 sessions/user, 10GB scrollback/user.

findings.question: STRIDE threat modeling application
findings.answer: STRIDE analysis: (S)poofing: master/client impersonation (cert pinning, SSH keys), DNS spoofing (DNSSEC); (T)ampering: message tampering (TLS 1.3 AEAD, DTLS SRTP), scrollback tampering (SQLite integrity, AES-256-GCM), JWT tampering (HMAC-SHA256); (R)epudiation: client denies input (audit log + SHA-256 hash), admin denies config (append-only log + S3 export); (I)nfo disclosure: scrollback leakage (encrypted at rest), traffic sniffing (TLS 1.3, PFS ECDHE), memory dump (zeroize crate, mlock); (D)oS: connection flood (rate limit, SYN cookies), storage exhaustion (quotas, LRU, zstd compression); (E)levation: read→write (RBAC checks), PTY escape (Linux namespaces, seccomp-bpf, AppArmor/SELinux). 15 threats across 6 STRIDE categories.

findings.question: P2P-specific security threats
findings.answer: 7 unique P2P threats: (1) NAT traversal exploitation: hole-punching exposes master port (mitigate: iptables DROP, UPnP disabled); (2) STUN/TURN abuse: DDoS amplification, $0.10/GB relay cost (limit 1GB/hour/client); (3) DHT poisoning: fake master records (Ed25519 signatures, 5min TTL, reputation threshold 3); (4) Sybil attack: 1000+ fake nodes (20-bit PoW, bootstrap nodes); (5) Eclipse attack: isolate master (5+ bootstrap DCs, peer diversity max 10%/subnet); (6) Relay eavesdropping: metadata leaks (E2EE mandatory, padding 0-256 bytes, rotate relay 1 hour); (7) DHT metadata leakage: IP→master correlation (dummy queries 2:1 ratio, Tor support). P2P adds +15k LOC, +5 deps, +7 threats, +$50/month TURN cost. Alternative: HTTPS relay-only reduces to 2 threats, -10k LOC, -$40/month. Recommendation: P2P optional (--p2p-mode flag), default HTTPS relay.

findings.question: Mitigations and security controls
findings.answer: 6-layer defense: (1) Input validation: JSON Schema (depth 5, props 50), length limits (UUID 36, username 64, msg 1MB), regex sanitization; (2) Rate limiting: token bucket (100 msg/min, 1000 conn/hour, 5 auth fail→1h block), governor crate, Redis state; (3) Resource quotas: cgroups v2 (100MB mem, 1 CPU, 10GB disk per session), 10GB scrollback/user, 100 sessions/user, systemd-run enforcement; (4) Audit logging: CEF format, 21 event types (auth, authz, session, admin, security, data access), SQLite append-only, 90d retention (1yr PCI, 7yr HIPAA), hourly syslog export, HMAC-SHA256 integrity; (5) Intrusion detection: brute force (5 fail→block), anomaly (z-score >3, 7d baseline), signature (CVE regex, AbuseIPDB), auto-block iptables + alerts; (6) Incident response: runbooks for compromised master/client, DDoS, breach (GDPR 72h notification).
